title: The participle as a verb, and compound tenses

objectives.can: Read a participle as the main verb of a clause, and הֲוָה with a participle as continued or repeated action.

explanation.summary: In Biblical Aramaic the participle is often the main verb of a clause. It narrates past events (עָנֵה וְאָמַר, 'he answered and said'), states what is true now (אֲנָה חָזֵה, 'I see'), and with a form of הֲוָה, 'to be', describes an action that continued or was repeated in the past (חָזֵה הֲוֵית, 'I was looking').

sections.heading: A participle that is a verb
body: You have learned the participle as a verbal adjective that agrees with a noun in gender, number and state. In Aramaic it does more: it can stand alone as the predicate of a clause, so that it does the work of a finite verb. The participle then agrees with its subject. In Daniel 3:17 the three friends speak of אֱלָהַנָא דִּי אֲנַחְנָא פָלְחִין, 'our God whom we serve': אֲנַחְנָא is the subject, 'we', and פָלְחִין is a masculine plural participle agreeing with it.

The subject may be a pronoun before or after the participle, a noun, or only the participle's own ending. In Daniel 3:25 the king says אֲנָה חָזֵה גֻּבְרִין אַרְבְּעָה, 'I see four men'. In Daniel 3:16 the order is reversed: לָא חַשְׁחִין אֲנַחְנָה, 'we have no need'. In Daniel 2:8 the king says to the Chaldeans אַנְתּוּן זָבְנִין עִדָּנָא, 'you are gaining time'. Finally, God's regular acts are told with participles: in Daniel 2:21 וְהוּא מְהַשְׁנֵא עִדָּנַיָּא וְזִמְנַיָּא, 'it is he who changes the times and the seasons'.

The form does not itself say when. Grammarians describe the Aramaic participle as unmarked for time: the time comes from the setting. In a speech about the present it is present, and in a story it is past.

sections.heading: The participle in a story
body: Narrative often moves along on participles. The commonest sign is the opening of a speech: עָנֵה וְאָמַר, literally 'answering and saying', which means 'he answered and said' (Daniel 3:14, 3:19, 3:26). Both words are masculine singular participles. For a plural speaker the pair is עָנַיִן וְאָמְרִין in Daniel 3:24. Sometimes the first is a perfect and the second a participle: in Daniel 3:16 עֲנוֹ שַׁדְרַךְ מֵישַׁךְ וַעֲבֵד נְגוֹ וְאָמְרִין לְמַלְכָּא means 'Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego answered and said to the king', and עֲנוֹ is a perfect (plural) and וְאָמְרִין a participle. The sense is the same.

Other events are told the same way. In Daniel 3:7 כְּדִי שָׁמְעִין כָּל עַמְמַיָּא קָל קַרְנָא is 'when all the peoples heard the sound of the horn', and the verse goes on with נָפְלִין and סָגְדִין, 'they fell down and worshipped'. All three are participles, and all three describe past events. In Daniel 3:26 בֵּאדַיִן נָפְקִין שַׁדְרַךְ מֵישַׁךְ וַעֲבֵד נְגוֹ is 'then Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego came out'. Here the word בֵּאדַיִן ('then') ties the participle to the story.

sections.heading: הֲוָה with a participle
body: To say that an action was going on or was repeated in the past, Aramaic puts the perfect of הֲוָה, 'to be', beside the participle. The participle gives the action; הֲוָה places it in the past. The two agree with the subject in person, gender and number, and the participle may come first or second.

In the visions of Daniel the narrator says again and again חָזֵה הֲוֵית, 'I was looking', and then tells what he saw (Daniel 7:2, 7:4, 7:6, 7:7). In Daniel 2:31 the same words are addressed to the king: אַנְתְּה מַלְכָּא חָזֵה הֲוַיְתָ, 'you, O king, were looking'. In Daniel 4:26 מְהַלֵּךְ הֲוָה says that the king 'was walking' on the royal palace of Babylon. In Daniel 6:5 the officials הֲווֹ בָעַיִן, 'were seeking' a ground for accusation: the plural verb and the plural participle both show the plural subject.

Repeated or habitual action is told the same way. Daniel 6:11 says that Daniel prayed three times a day, 'as he had been doing' before: כָּל קֳבֵל דִּי הֲוָא עָבֵד. Daniel 5:19 says that Nebuchadnezzar acted as he pleased: דִּי הֲוָה צָבֵא הֲוָא קָטֵל, 'whom he wished, he would kill'.

sections.heading: Reading a participle in context
body: When you meet a participle as the last or only verb in a clause, ask three questions. Who is the subject? Read the participle's gender and number and look for a noun or pronoun that agrees, or take the ending alone. Is הֲוָה present? If so, the clause is in the past and the action is continued or repeated. If not, look at the story: is it a speech (present), or a narrative (past)?

Remember also that the participle is still a participle. Passive participles are used as predicates too: in Daniel 3:25 שְׁרַיִן, 'loosed', describes the men walking in the fire. Look at the stem and voice on the word, not only at its ending.

misunderstandings: A participle is not always a present tense. In Daniel 3:7 the three participles שָׁמְעִין, נָפְלִין and סָגְדִין report events that had happened.
עָנֵה וְאָמַר is not a perfect and an infinitive. Both words are participles; the ending shows only the number and gender of the speaker.
הֲוָה with a participle is not a simple 'he was'. Together they say that the action was going on or was repeated: 'he was walking', 'I was looking'.
A participle with a noun is not always an adjective. In אֲנָה חָזֵה, 'I see', there is no noun for it to describe: the participle is the verb.

deeper.heading: Looking ahead
body: This use goes further than the usual use in Hebrew, where the participle mostly names or describes someone who does something, or states what is happening now. In later Aramaic, and above all in Syriac, the participle becomes the ordinary present tense, and a pronoun is attached to it to show the person. Many grammarians see the Aramaic of Daniel and Ezra as an early stage of that development. The perfect is still common for plain past events in these stories, so you will meet both in the same chapter.

reading.why: The vision of the four beasts is told with participles throughout: חָזֵה הֲוֵית, 'I was looking', returns as a refrain, and the animals rise and differ from one another in participles. You can watch the participle as a verb and the compound tense at work in a single chapter.

segments.title: Daniel
segments.english: Daniel spoke and said: I saw in my vision by night, and, behold, the four winds of the heaven broke forth upon the great sea.
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Daniel
segments.english: And four great beasts came up from the sea, diverse one from another.
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Daniel
segments.english: The first was like a lion, and had eagle's wings; I beheld till the wings thereof were plucked off, and it was lifted up from the earth, and made stand upon two feet as a man, and a man's heart was given to it.

segments.title: Daniel
segments.english: And behold another beast, a second, like to a bear, and it raised up itself on one side, and it had three ribs in its mouth between its teeth; and it was said thus unto it: 'Arise, devour much flesh.'
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Daniel
segments.english: After this I beheld, and lo another, like a leopard, which had upon the sides of it four wings of a fowl; the beast had also four heads; and dominion was given to it.

segments.title: Daniel
segments.english: After this I saw in the night visions, and behold a fourth beast, dreadful and terrible, and strong exceedingly; and it had great iron teeth; it devoured and broke in pieces, and stamped the residue with its feet; and it was diverse from all the beasts that were before it; and it had ten horns.
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Daniel
segments.english: I considered the horns, and, behold, there came up among them another horn, a little one, before which three of the first horns were plucked up by the roots; and, behold, in this horn were eyes like the eyes of a man, and a mouth speaking great things.

segments.title: Daniel
segments.english: I beheld till thrones were placed, and one that was ancient of days did sit: his raiment was as white snow, and the hair of his head like pure wool; his throne was fiery flames, and the wheels thereof burning fire.
